extracted.intended_audience: writers—especially humor writers, copywriters, and content marketers
extracted.subtask_description: Ten practical, transferable writing principles from The Onion’s founding editor aimed at crafting memorable satire and attention-grabbing online copy; applicable to headlines, articles, scripts, and sales copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept is king
rubrics_metrics.description: Your concept (headline/title) must make the piece stand out and grab attention; put the joke or core idea first so readers are hooked before they invest time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an attention economy the headline is the 'shingle on your door' — if it isn't the right concept you're sunk before writing. Choose concepts that speak to the target audience’s pleasures or pains. Historically The Onion relied on striking headlines to attract passersby; online, a headline that promises to answer a burning question or address a personal problem drives clicks and reads.

rubrics_metrics.name: The key to quality is quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate a very large number of ideas because most will be poor; quality emerges from abundance and selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Onion had writers produce ~20 headlines each for weekly meetings; teams review hundreds of ideas and publish only a dozen or so. Professionals work from abundance (late-night monologues use the same method). Expect ~95% of output to be garbage and rely on volume to surface the best material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorter is better: remove superfluous words and even syllables to make writing punchier and clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing should seek reduction; cutting a single syllable can improve a joke. Trimming fat reveals the core message and sometimes shows you had nothing to say—better to discover that early. Conciseness applies across genres, not just comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruffle some feathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective satire often offends or challenges power; content that angers or pushes buttons is more likely to be remembered than gentle, toothless humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast Horatian (light, inoffensive) vs Juvenalian (biting, critical) satire: Horatian may amuse briefly but won't live in cultural memory; Juvenalian addresses social evils and speaks truth to power. Be clear on your message and goal before deciding how provocative to be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t fall in love (kill your darlings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be willing to discard ideas you're attached to; don't treat a single idea as your identity or refuse constructive feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New writers often overvalue each idea because they have few; attachment leads to defensiveness and stalls improvement. Take feedback, move on quickly, and prioritize serving readers over protecting personal favorites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete, sensory-specific detail to create clear mental images and evoke emotions; specificity improves clarity without requiring verbosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific details help readers feel an emotion and visualize scenes—e.g., Salinger’s concise lines that nonetheless convey vivid context. Specificity aids engagement and can drive readers to action (laugh, like, buy). It doesn't mean long descriptions—precise, crisp imagery is the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful proofreading signals professionalism; grammar, spelling, and syntax errors undermine credibility and cost opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you're talented, submission packets with mistakes will be passed over for cleaner competitors. Proofreading is an easy way to improve chances of getting hired or accepted and to convey seriousness to editors and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don’t tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer showing characters’ traits and situations through actions, examples, or analogies rather than directly stating them; showing engages readers and elicits emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling (‘Bob is mean’) is less effective than showing (‘Bob just stabbed a baby through the heart!’) — the article uses an extreme example to make the point. Use examples, analogies, and literary devices to hide the explicit message and let readers arrive at the meaning themselves for greater engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Write so readers of many levels can understand and engage with your work; avoid density, unnecessary complexity, and prerequisites for comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your work should be an easy on-ramp; rely on references people can grasp without caveats. In the modern attention economy, authorial intent or requiring interpretation is a liability—clarity is the writer’s responsibility. Ask, 'How can I make this more clear?' when unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your joke and make sure the reader knows your joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Be in control of your piece’s structure and subtext: understand the joke’s subtext, filters, and timing so the audience laughs at the intended target at the right moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about your point in structure (tell them what you’ll say, say it, then tell them you said it). As a humor writer you must organize the joke so readers perceive the subtext and apply the intended 'funny filters.' This principle generalizes to all writing: know your topic, audience, and purpose and control the reader’s experience like a puppeteer or a master filmmaker.
